passages.t: A little folly, and the world turned upside down
passages.happening:
‘As dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil, so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor’ (verse 1). ‘A wise man’s heart inclines to the right, but the heart of a fool to the left’ (verse 2). Even walking down the road the fool shows everyone that he is a fool (verse 3).

‘If the ruler’s temper flares against you, do not abandon your post, for calmness lays great offenses to rest’ (verse 4).

Then an evil the Teacher has seen, an error that comes from the ruler (verse 5): fools are set in high places while the capable sit low (verse 6). ‘I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 9 ended with a warning that one sinner destroys much good. Chapter 10 takes that saying and multiplies it into a collection of proverbs about how folly spoils what wisdom builds. The Teacher sounds much like Proverbs here, but with his own edge: he knows the world does not always reward the wise.

Perfumer's oil was costly and carefully made, and a few dead flies could ruin a whole batch. A little folly can spoil a great deal of wisdom.

In verse 2 the right hand was the side of strength, skill and favor in the ancient world, and the left often the side of weakness or misfortune. The verse has nothing to do with modern political labels.

Verses 5 to 7 describe the court turned upside down: the foolish promoted, the able passed over, slaves riding while princes walk.
passages.later: Proverbs says the same of a world out of order: ‘Luxury is unseemly for a fool’ (Proverbs 19:10), and among the things under which the earth trembles is ‘a servant who becomes king’ (Proverbs 30:22).
passages.asks: A little folly can spoil much wisdom. Ask what small habit or careless word could undo the good you have built. And ask where calmness, as verse 4 says, could quiet an offense you are tempted to answer in anger.

passages.t: The risks of work, and the advantage of skill
passages.happening:
‘He who digs a pit may fall into it, and he who breaches a wall may be bitten by a snake’ (verse 8). ‘The one who quarries stones may be injured by them, and he who splits logs endangers himself’ (verse 9). ‘If the axe is dull and the blade unsharpened, more strength must be exerted, but skill produces success’ (verse 10). ‘If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer’ (verse 11).

‘The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious, but the lips of a fool consume him’ (verse 12). His talk begins in folly and ends in evil madness (verse 13). ‘Yet the fool multiplies words’ (verse 14), though no one knows what is coming. ‘The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
These sayings come from ordinary work: digging pits, breaking through old walls where snakes nested, quarrying stone, splitting logs. Each had real risks.

Snake charming was practiced in the ancient world, and the Old Testament mentions it elsewhere. A charmer bitten before he could work his charm gained nothing from his skill. Advantage, yitron, a key word of the book, ends the cluster: skill gives an advantage, if it is used in time.

The fool's speech starts in folly and ends in madness, and he talks most about what he knows least. He is so tired by his own work that he cannot even find the road into town.
passages.later: The psalms know the charmer: the wicked are like a deaf cobra, ‘refusing to hear the tune of the charmer who skillfully weaves his spell’ (Psalm 58:5). And Proverbs agrees with verse 12: ‘A fool’s mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare to his soul’ (Proverbs 18:7).
passages.asks: A dull axe needs more strength, and skill brings success. Ask where a little preparation, sharpening the axe, would save you much wasted effort. And ask where your words have been more than the matter needed.

passages.t: Rulers, a leaking roof, and a bird that carries words
passages.happening:
‘Woe to you, O land whose king is a youth, and whose princes feast in the morning’ (verse 16). But a land is well off whose king is of noble birth and whose princes eat at the proper time, ‘for strength and not for drunkenness’ (verse 17).

‘Through laziness the roof caves in, and in the hands of the idle, the house leaks’ (verse 18). ‘A feast is prepared for laughter, and wine makes life merry, but money is the answer for everything’ (verse 19).

‘Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, or curse the rich even in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report your speech’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Verse 16 recalls moments when inexperience led to disaster. After Solomon died, his son Rehoboam listened to the young men he had grown up with instead of the elders, and the kingdom split. The Hebrew word for youth, na'ar, can also mean servant, so some readers hear verse 16 as a king of low birth set against the son of nobles in verse 17. Feasting in the morning was a mark of a wasted life.

Flat roofs of beams and packed clay needed constant care. Neglect them, and the rain came in.

The bird of the air that carries words is an ancient version of the saying that walls have ears.
passages.later: Isaiah warns the morning feasters of verse 16: ‘Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink’ (Isaiah 5:11). And the kingdom split when Rehoboam ‘rejected the advice of the elders’ (1 Kings 12:13).
passages.hard:
Does verse 19 really teach that money is the answer for everything?

Verse 19 says that a feast is prepared for laughter, wine makes life merry, but money is the answer for everything. Interpreters read it in several ways.

Some take it as ironic, the voice of the self-indulgent princes of verse 16 who feast in the morning and think money solves every problem. Then the Teacher is quoting a foolish attitude in order to expose it. Others take it as a plain observation: money answers to, or pays for, all these things, since feasts and wine must be paid for. The Hebrew verb can mean to answer or to respond to, which allows both readings.

What is clear from the book as a whole is that the Teacher does not believe money satisfies (5:10) or survives death (5:15). Whatever this proverb means, it is not the book's final word about wealth.
passages.asks: A neglected roof caves in a little at a time. Ask what in your house, or your life, is slowly leaking through neglect. And ask what you say in private that you would not want carried abroad.
